title: Symptoms We Treat
shortDescription: Common neurological symptoms and the clinic services that can help you find out more.
introduction: This page lists common neurological symptoms and the clinic services that may be relevant to them. It is a guide to help you know where to start; it cannot tell you the cause of your symptoms.
If you are not sure which service you need, a general neurology consultation is a good place to begin.

items.text: Weakness, numbness or speech problems that came and went
Tremor, stiffness or slowness of movement
Numbness, tingling or burning in the hands or feet
Back or neck pain spreading into an arm or leg
Difficulty walking or doing daily tasks after a neurological illness

sections.heading: Symptoms that need emergency care
sections.intro: Do not wait for an appointment. Call 112 or go to the nearest emergency department if you notice:
items: Sudden weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, especially on one side
Sudden difficulty speaking or understanding speech
A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery in between
A sudden, severe 'worst-ever' headache
Loss of consciousness or sudden confusion
Weakness that is spreading quickly, or difficulty breathing or swallowing

faqs.question: Can this page tell me what is causing my symptoms?
faqs.answer: No. Symptoms can have many causes. Only an assessment by a doctor can work out the cause and the right treatment.

title: First Visit Guide
shortDescription: What usually happens at your first appointment and how to make the most of it.
introduction: Your first visit is a chance to explain your symptoms, ask questions and agree on the next steps. This guide explains what usually happens and how to make the most of your appointment.

sections.heading: Before your visit
items: Book an appointment by calling the clinic or sending a WhatsApp message. Walk-ins are welcome, but appointments are preferred.
Check which clinic you will visit and its OPD day and timings (Patna).

items.text: Gather your reports, scans and a list of your medicines.

items: Write down your symptoms and the questions you want to ask.

sections.heading: During your visit
items: The doctor will ask about your symptoms, medical history and medicines.
A physical and neurological examination is usually carried out.
Your previous reports and scans will be reviewed.
The doctor will explain the possible causes and whether any tests are needed.

sections.heading: After your visit
items: You may be advised to have tests, start treatment or begin therapy.
Keep your prescription and any test referrals safe.
Book a follow-up visit if one is advised.
Contact the clinic if your symptoms change or you have questions.

sections.heading: Clinic locations and OPD timings
sections.intro: Please confirm the OPD day and timings when you book.

faqs.question: Do I need an appointment?
faqs.answer: Walk-ins are welcome, but appointments are preferred at the Patna clinic.

faqs.question: Can a family member come with me?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member or caregiver can help describe your symptoms and remember the advice given.

title: What to Bring
shortDescription: A checklist of documents and information to bring to your appointment.
introduction: Bringing the right documents and information helps the doctor understand your history and avoids repeating tests unnecessarily.

sections.heading: Documents and records
items: Previous medical reports and doctors' letters
MRI or CT scan films or digital copies, together with the written reports
Hospital discharge summaries
Current and previous prescriptions
Test results such as blood tests, EEG, NCV/NCS or EMG reports

sections.heading: Information about you
items: A list of all the medicines you take, with doses and timings
Any allergies or previous reactions to medicines
Other medical conditions, such as diabetes or high blood pressure
A short diary of your symptoms, if you have kept one
A short phone video of episodes that come and go, such as seizures or abnormal movements, if it can be recorded safely

sections.heading: Also helpful
items: A family member or caregiver, especially for memory problems or seizures
Reading glasses and hearing aids, if you use them
Any walking aid you use
A list of the questions you want to ask

faqs.question: Should I bring the original scan films?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you have them. Bring the films or digital copies of the images as well as the written reports.

faqs.question: What if I do not have my old reports?
faqs.answer: Bring whatever you have. The doctor can still assess you and will advise whether any tests need to be repeated.

title: Test Preparation
shortDescription: General advice to help you prepare for neurological tests.
introduction: Preparation depends on the test. Always follow the specific instructions given by the clinic or the testing centre when you book. The general advice below applies to most neurological tests.

sections.heading: General advice
items: Ask the clinic when you book whether your test needs any special preparation
Do not stop or change any medicine unless your doctor advises you to
Bring previous test reports and scans
Tell the clinic if you have a pacemaker or metal implants, take blood-thinning medicines, have a bleeding disorder, may be pregnant or have allergies
Wear comfortable, loose clothing

faqs.question: Can I eat before my test?
faqs.answer: Ask the clinic when you book. Instructions vary between tests, so follow the advice given for your specific test.

faqs.question: Should I take my usual medicines on the day of the test?
faqs.answer: Continue your usual medicines unless the doctor tells you otherwise.

title: Emergency Guidance
shortDescription: Warning signs that need emergency care, and what to do while waiting for help.
urgentNotice: In an emergency, call 112 or go to the nearest emergency department immediately. Do not wait for a clinic appointment, and do not rely on this website.
introduction: Some neurological symptoms need emergency treatment, and acting quickly can make a big difference. If you notice any of the warning signs below, get emergency help straight away.

sections.heading: Signs of a stroke – think FAST
items: Face: one side of the face droops or the smile is uneven
Arm: weakness or numbness in one arm or leg
Speech: slurred speech, or difficulty speaking or understanding
Time: call 112 immediately and note the time the symptoms started

sections.heading: Other emergency warning signs
items: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery in between
A sudden, severe 'worst-ever' headache
A headache with fever, a stiff neck, confusion or a rash
Loss of consciousness or new confusion
Vomiting, drowsiness, confusion or a seizure after a head injury
Weakness that is spreading quickly, or difficulty breathing or swallowing
Back pain with loss of bladder or bowel control, or numbness around the genitals or buttocks

sections.heading: While waiting for help
items: Note the time the symptoms started.
Do not give food or drink to someone who may be having a stroke or is drowsy.
During a seizure, protect the person from injury, cushion their head and turn them onto their side once the jerking stops. Do not put anything in their mouth.
Keep a list of the person's medicines ready for the emergency team.

faqs.question: Should I contact the clinic in an emergency?
faqs.answer: In an emergency, call 112 or go to the nearest emergency department first. The clinic can help with follow-up care afterwards.

seoDescription: Neurological warning signs that need emergency care, including stroke (FAST) and prolonged seizures, and what to do while waiting for help.

title: Caregiver Guides
shortDescription: Practical tips for families and caregivers supporting someone with a neurological condition.
introduction: Caring for someone with a neurological condition can be rewarding, but it can also be demanding. These general tips can help you support your loved one and look after yourself.

sections.heading: Supporting appointments
items: Keep a folder of reports, prescriptions and scans
Note changes in symptoms, sleep, mood and behaviour between visits
Prepare questions before each appointment
Go with the person to appointments, if possible

sections.heading: Medicines
items: Keep an up-to-date list of all medicines and doses
Use a pill organiser or reminders to avoid missed doses
Do not stop or change medicines without medical advice
Report possible side effects to the doctor

sections.heading: Safety at home
items: Reduce fall risks: good lighting, no loose rugs and handrails where needed
Supervise cooking, medicines and money for people with memory problems
Learn seizure first aid if the person has epilepsy
Keep emergency numbers, including 112, easy to find

sections.heading: Looking after yourself
items: Take regular breaks and share responsibilities with other family members.
Talk to someone you trust about how you are feeling.
Look after your own health, sleep and appointments.

faqs.question: How can I help someone with memory problems?
faqs.answer: Keep routines simple and consistent, use calendars and reminders, speak calmly in short sentences and make the home safe.

faqs.question: When should I seek urgent help?
faqs.answer: Call 112 for emergency warning signs such as sudden weakness, difficulty speaking, a long seizure or loss of consciousness.
